headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper - and does not describe either condition in general.

Both papers show substantial work and employment disability, but the Lyme disease paper relies on self-reported disability status while the Long COVID paper uses objective exercise-testing thresholds, so the two are not directly comparable numbers.
Neither paper reports any dollar-denominated medical, non-medical, or indirect cost figures, so no out-of-pocket or total-expenditure comparison can be made from this evidence.

comparison_rows.dimension: Work and income loss / employment impact

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 35% of persistent Lyme disease patients self-identified as disabled as their main form of work, with a 6 percentage-point gap favoring higher disability among women (36%) versus men (30%); it also found 61% spent 8+ days in bed over six months, but no dollar-denominated wage-loss figures are given.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports that 66.3% of a severe, occupationally-selected post-COVID cohort met objective exercise-testing (CPET) thresholds for absolute work disability, while only 25% were working or in work reintegration; no dollar-denominated wage-loss figures are given either.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers independently document major employment disability, though they measure it in very different ways (self-report versus objective physiological testing), so readers should not treat the percentages as equivalent.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper finds 55% of patients experienced a 3-or-more-year delay from symptom onset to diagnosis, with women delayed more often than men by 8 percentage points.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not measure diagnostic delay at all; its inclusion criteria actually required patients to already have a formal diagnosis code before enrollment, so delay to diagnosis is not something this paper's evidence can speak to.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic delay is a clearly documented burden in the Lyme disease paper but is simply absent as a measured topic in the Long COVID paper, so no genuine cross-condition comparison is possible here.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that 76% of patients were misdiagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition before their Lyme diagnosis, with a 15 percentage-point gap showing this happened more often to women.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report rates of misdiagnosis with other conditions; it instead describes a related but distinct problem, that organ-centered clinical tests routinely come back unremarkable in severely affected patients, leaving their disability objectively undocumented until CPET testing was used.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers describe forms of clinical disbelief or diagnostic failure, but the specific pattern differs: explicit alternative-diagnosis labeling in Lyme disease versus inconclusive standard testing in Long COVID, so this is a related but not identical burden.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper does not tag or report an administrative-recognition gap between how patients experience disability and how any formal system recognizes it.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper finds that the share of patients meeting the objective CPET disability threshold (66.3%) differs from the share formally on sick leave by -8.7 percentage points, meaning more patients were on sick leave than strictly met the objective disability threshold.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper directly measures a gap between objective functional testing and formal administrative disability status, which is relevant to insurance and occupational-disease recognition processes.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no direct medical or non-medical cost figures anywhere; it explicitly states that out-of-pocket spending, caregiver costs, and travel costs are not mentioned or measured.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper likewise reports no dollar-denominated cost data of any kind, and notes that financial concerns are only mentioned as a reason patients keep working, without being quantified.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave out-of-pocket and direct cost burden completely unmeasured, so no simulator built from either source alone can answer questions about dollar costs to patients.

comparison_rows.dimension: How official or administrative data may undercount the condition

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper notes that the CDC's cited estimate of 476,000 new diagnoses per year is drawn from commercial insurance claims data, which the paper flags as a different and non-comparable ascertainment method from its own self-reported patient registry.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's cohort was pre-selected on already having received a formal ICD-10 diagnosis code from a physician, which the paper itself flags as a mechanism that could exclude symptomatic patients who never obtained that code.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers independently flag that reliance on administrative or claims-based diagnosis pathways can undercount the true affected population, a shared structural limitation.

comparison_rows.dimension: Subgroup disaggregation (beyond the single axis each paper studied)

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper disaggregates findings by sex only, and the authors themselves state the sample lacked sufficient racial/ethnic or gender-spectrum diversity to assess those subgroups.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper disaggregates findings only by ME/CFS status and multimorbidity, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or other subgroups despite the cohort being 88% female.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave most demographic subgroup variation unexamined, limiting how far either paper's findings can be generalized to diverse patient populations.

comparison_rows.dimension: What the evidence leaves unmeasured in terms of financial burden

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper leaves indirect costs (wage loss in dollar terms), long-term financial consequences like debt, and insurance claim outcomes completely unmeasured, despite reporting disability and bed-day findings that imply a productivity impact.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper leaves occupational-disease compensation amounts and outcomes of the insurance recognition process unmeasured, despite recruiting patients specifically through that occupational-insurance pathway.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers document functional and occupational burden strongly but stop short of translating it into any financial outcome, leaving a persistent blind spot in both evidence bases.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper reports any dollar-denominated direct medical, direct non-medical, or indirect cost figures, despite both describing disability that plausibly carries financial consequences.

evidence.note: States explicitly that no cost, caregiver burden, travel cost, or insurance data are reported anywhere in the Lyme disease paper.
States explicitly that no dollar-denominated cost data of any kind appear anywhere in the Long COVID paper, despite recruitment through an occupational-insurance pathway.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers document substantial work and employment disability within their specific patient populations, though measured through different methods.

evidence.note: 35% of persistent Lyme disease patients self-identified as disabled as their main form of work.
66.3% of the severe post-COVID cohort met objective CPET thresholds for absolute work disability.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers disaggregate their findings along only one demographic or clinical axis, leaving most other subgroup variation unexamined.

evidence.note: Disaggregates only by sex and states the sample lacked diversity to examine race/ethnicity or gender-spectrum subgroups.
Disaggregates only by ME/CFS status and multimorbidity, with no breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity despite an 88% female cohort.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers flag that their underlying population was shaped by an administrative or claims-based pathway that could undercount the true affected population.

evidence.note: Notes the CDC's cited 476,000-per-year estimate comes from commercial insurance claims data rather than prospective surveillance.
Notes the cohort was pre-selected on already having a formal ICD-10 diagnosis code, which could exclude undiagnosed symptomatic patients.

condition_specific_themes.theme: Women with persistent Lyme disease experience markedly longer diagnostic delay and far more frequent misdiagnosis with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric conditions than men.

evidence.note: Reports a 15 percentage-point sex gap in CFS/fibromyalgia/psychiatric misdiagnosis and an 8 percentage-point sex gap in 3+ year diagnostic delay.

condition_specific_themes.theme: In this severe post-COVID cohort, standard organ-centered clinical diagnostics routinely come back unremarkable, so objective exercise testing was introduced specifically to document disability that would otherwise remain invisible.

evidence.note: Describes organ-centered diagnostics 'frequently fail to explain' work disability, motivating the CPET-based approach used in this paper.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper found a gap between how many patients met an objective disability threshold and how many were formally on sick leave, a type of administrative-recognition mismatch not addressed in the Lyme disease paper.

evidence.note: Reports a -8.7 percentage-point gap between the objective CPET disability rate (66.3%) and the sick-leave rate.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper measures caregiver burden, travel costs, paid help, or other non-medical cost categories, despite both describing disability that plausibly affects household finances.
Neither paper tracks long-term financial consequences such as debt, bankruptcy, or insurance claim denials for the condition it studies.
Neither paper offers longitudinal follow-up linking its functional or diagnostic findings to financial outcomes over time; both are cross-sectional or retrospective snapshots.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers - one on persistent Lyme disease and one on severe post-COVID condition - and does not describe either condition in general. Both papers document real, serious functional and employment burden in their specific patient populations, but they measure burden in different ways (self-reported sex-stratified rates in the Lyme disease paper, objective exercise-testing thresholds in the Long COVID paper), and neither reports any dollar-denominated cost figures at all. The clearest shared pattern is an evidence gap: both papers describe disability-level impairment without any accompanying financial data, and both disaggregate their findings along only one axis (sex for Lyme disease, ME/CFS status for Long COVID), leaving most demographic subgroups unexamined. Where the papers diverge, it is mainly in what each one chose to measure - diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis for Lyme disease, objective functional capacity and sick-leave status for Long COVID - rather than in any conflicting finding about the same measure.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison covers two papers only (one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper), with no papers overlapping both conditions and none in the unconfirmed set; each condition's evidence base here is a single, small, non-randomly selected document, not a representative or controlled sample of either condition, so no general conclusions about Lyme disease or Long COVID as a whole can be drawn from this comparison.

learning_error: Learning card cites a figure that is not one of that paper's own: disabled_main_work_status_gap_pct_points

learning_cards.headline: Misdiagnosis as psychiatric or CFS differs by sex in Lyme disease
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found a 15 percentage point gap (women minus men) in being misdiagnosed with CFS, fibromyalgia, or a psychiatric condition.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any misdiagnosis rates, let alone broken down by sex.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID clinics compare how often women versus men are misdiagnosed with a psychiatric condition before their diagnosis is confirmed?

learning_cards.headline: Diagnostic delay and clinician-shopping differ by sex in Lyme disease
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found an 8 percentage point gap (women minus men) in having a diagnostic delay of 3 or more years, and an 11 percentage point gap in having seen 10 or more clinicians before diagnosis.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not measure time-to-diagnosis or number of clinicians seen before diagnosis at all.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers track diagnostic delay and clinician-visit counts separately for women and men in their cohort?

learning_cards.headline: Objective test results and sick-leave status can disagree
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found a -8.7 percentage point gap between the objective CPET disability rate and the sick-leave rate, meaning more patients were on sick leave than met the objective disability threshold.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not use objective exercise-capacity testing or compare it against administrative work-leave status.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers compare results from an objective functional test against patients' formal work-leave status?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper points Long COVID researchers toward checking whether diagnostic delay, clinician-shopping, and misdiagnosis differ by sex, while the Long COVID paper points Lyme disease researchers toward pairing objective functional testing with administrative work status and examining multimorbidity by condition subtype.
